problems.description: Commits the entire compiled build/ directory (cli.js, generator.js, .d.ts, source maps) to source control; generated output should be gitignored and produced by a build step, otherwise every source change creates noisy diffs and drift risk.

Convention score of 0.47 with 3048 violations (camelCase/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE on cache.d.ts, cli.d.ts, etc.); while much of this is Sonar flagging auto-generated .d.ts files, the root cause is tracking generated artifacts instead of excluding them.
Cognitive complexity +110 and smells +10 in a greenfield commit, suggesting the generator/parser logic should be split into smaller helpers rather than monolithic render functions.
Duplications of 1.6% introduced immediately — tag/date rendering is repeated across renderPageHtml and renderIndexHtml and should be extracted.
htmlEncode escapes &, <, >, " but not the single quote, which can leave attribute-context injection holes; escaping ' too is the defensive convention.

strengths: Zero bugs and no external runtime dependencies (only Node built-ins fs/path).
Straightforward, readable argument parsing with a clear usage string for unknown commands.
User-provided content (titles, tags, dates) is consistently HTML-escaped before rendering.
Directory recursion and output mkdir with recursive:true make the pipeline robust to missing paths.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, dependency-free minimal SSG, but it should not have committed compiled build artifacts — that single decision is what drags the convention score to 0.47 and constitutes the main debt.

problems.description: Commit ships generated build artifacts (build/*.js, *.js.map, *.d.ts) and the low 0.47 convention score is entirely driven by naming violations in auto-generated declaration files (cache.d.ts, cli.d.ts) — a measurement artifact, but committing build output bloats diffs and will keep inflating convention checks.
loadTemplates/registerPartials repeat the same existsSync/readdirSync/filter('.hbs')/readFileSync/compile block three times (partials, layouts, page templates), matching the +2 SonarQube smells.
Single commit is large (+590/-42 lines across 7 files) mixing CLI parsing, generator signature change, and a new Handlebars engine, plus regenerated sourcemaps.

strengths: Backwards-compatible feature: templateDir is an optional parameter so existing generateSite callers are unaffected
Cognitive complexity decreased by 5 with zero new bugs and no duplications
Usage string updated alongside the new --templates flag so docs stay in sync
Clean separation of partials, layouts, and page templates in the Handlebars integration
commit_reviews.summary: Adds a backward-compatible --templates feature with lower cognitive complexity and no new bugs, but commits generated build artifacts whose .d.ts naming violations account for the low 0.47 convention score.

problems.description: The parseDirectory + generateSite + console.log block is duplicated verbatim in both the 'build' and 'serve' branches instead of being factored into a shared helper — matches the +2.9% duplication delta.

SonarQube cognitive complexity +141 for a two-command CLI is disproportionate; the new server.ts (156 lines with rebuild/close plumbing) carries most of it and appears over-engineered for a static 'serve' feature.
Generated build artifacts (build/server.js, *.map, *.d.ts) are committed, which both inflates the diff (+761/-27) and sources the bulk of the 3048 convention violations in the .d.ts files.
port is assigned via parseInt without NaN/range validation, so `--port abc` silently yields an invalid port at runtime.

The +8 smells and convention score of 0.47 are largely driven by compiler-emitted .d.ts files (cli.d.ts, cache.d.ts: camelCase/PascalCase naming) rather than handwritten source — flagging as a measurement discrepancy.

strengths: Replaced unconditional CLI execution with explicit build/serve/usage dispatch, making the command contract clearer.
Server concerns are properly isolated in a new module rather than inlined into cli.js, respecting separation of concerns.
Reuses existing parseDirectory/generateSite entry points instead of reimplementing parsing logic.
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally sound feature (serve command + extracted server module) that fits the existing CLI architecture, but the duplicated build block, +141 cognitive complexity, and committed build artifacts add real technical debt.

problems.description: In the serve branch, `const pages = engine.pages` is captured before `await engine.build()` completes, so the logged page count reads a stale (likely empty) array; build branch reads `engine.pages.length` only after await, showing inconsistent async usage.
Refactor adds +179 cognitive complexity and +6 smells per SonarQube; a refactor that restructures the pipeline should reduce, not nearly double, complexity.

Convention score 0.47 with 3048 violations (camelCase/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE naming on cache.d.ts, cli.d.ts). Flagged discrepancy: these violations are on generated declaration/build files, so part of the low score may be measurement noise rather than authored code quality.
Build branch hardcodes `port: 3000` in the SSGEngine options even though serve-only config is irrelevant to build, leaving an unused/misleading config value.
loadConfigPlugins swallows all errors with a bare catch and silently falls back to defaults, which can mask a genuinely broken ssg.config.js during debugging.

strengths: Introduces a plugin-based SSGEngine architecture with clean extension points (markdown/template/devserver plugins) and config-file-driven plugin loading.
Refactors top-level logic into async main() with centralized error handling and a non-zero exit on failure.
Config loading correctly handles both CommonJS and default-export interop for ssg.config.js.
Good separation of concerns: engine orchestration, plugin registry, and parse/config helpers are distinct.
commit_reviews.summary: Sound architectural direction toward a plugin engine, but the refactor regresses with an async sequencing defect, a large cognitive-complexity increase, and low convention adherence, making it net worse than the structure it replaced.

problems.description: Convention score 0.47 with 3048 violations (camelCase/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE naming rules) across cache.d.ts, cli.d.ts and related files; bulk of the +1446 lines violates enforced naming conventions

Compiled output (build/cache.js, build/cache.d.ts, build/cache.d.ts.map, sourceMappingURL artifacts) is committed to git; generated artifacts should be gitignored and produced by the build step, and the low convention score is driven largely by lint running over these generated files
+1446 lines added with no tests in the diff; a BuildCache with content/template hashing and cache invalidation logic is exactly the kind of logic that needs unit coverage
load() and clear() swallow all exceptions via bare catch {}, silently masking corrupted-cache and I/O errors which complicates debugging cache failures
Cognitive complexity +7 with +1 class and +4 functions added in a single cross-cutting commit; mixing the cache feature with 24 new imports into one 1446-line change widens review surface

strengths: Content-addressable hashing (sha256 over file content) with a separate template hash is a sound incremental-build invalidation design
Template hash computation sorts directory entries, making the hash deterministic across filesystems
Corrupted or missing cache is handled gracefully by resetting to a fresh manifest instead of crashing the build
Cache manifest cleanly separates contentHashes, templateHash, and per-page/index HTML entries, making invalidation logic explicit
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cache-invalidation design but the commit is worse overall: convention score dropped to 0.47 with 3048 naming violations and generated build artifacts committed to git — a discrepancy worth noting is that the majority of the flagged violations land on compiled .d.ts files, so the 0.47 score is inflated by linting generated output rather than genuine source-style drift.

compounding_issues: Session 1's inline HTML rendering (renderPageHtml/renderIndexHtml) was never retired; Session 2 added a Handlebars engine as an alternative and sessions 3-5 kept both paths alive in generator.ts, leaving two competing rendering implementations to maintain.
Session 4's plugin refactor hard-couples serve() to a plugin named 'devserver' (engine.serve throws if not found) instead of depending on an interface, constraining how serving can be composed.

Session 4 moved page population into MarkdownPlugin.beforeBuild, so engine.pages stays empty until build() runs; the CLI's serve path reads engine.pages before the pipeline completes, a latent ordering fragility that persisted into session 5.
Session 5's incremental cache only activates when a template directory exists (requires templateHash !== ''), so the default no-templates path gets no build speedup.

Compiled build/*.js + source maps were committed from session 1 and node_modules (~12k lines) was committed in session 3, bloating the repo and compounding as every session re-touches generated artifacts.
key_decisions: S1 greenfield: discarded the Express Todo API seed entirely and built a markdown static site generator (parser via gray-matter/marked, generator, CLI) from scratch.
S2 feature_addition: adopted Handlebars as the template engine with layouts, partials, and per-page templates, while keeping inline HTML rendering as the fallback.
S3 integration: added a dev server using chokidar file watching + WebSocket live reload with path-traversal protection and a new 'serve' command.
S4 refactor: extracted an extensible plugin architecture (SSGEngine + onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd hooks) with Markdown/Template/DevServer plugins configured via ssg.config.

S5 cross_cutting: added an incremental build cache keyed on SHA-256 content and template hashes with two-tier invalidation (parser skips re-parse, generator skips re-render) plus stale-output cleanup.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions. Session 1 produced a minimal but clean MVP; session 2 added real templating with solid test growth (3 to 8 generator tests); session 3 integrated a full dev server with live reload and security guardrails; session 4 consolidated the growing monolith into a clean plugin architecture that made the system extensible; session 5 layered a sophisticated two-tier incremental cache (content hashes in the parser, template hashes in the generator) with a large 667-line test suite. The arc is a natural feature-addition-then-refactor rhythm, with the only regression risk being mild accumulated technical debt: dual rendering paths, committed build artifacts and node_modules, and a couple of coupling/ordering smells that the plugin refactor left behind.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc that progresses naturally from greenfield MVP through templating, dev-server integration, plugin refactor, and a well-tested cross-cutting cache, with quality improving each session despite mild accumulated hygiene debt.
